chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Term Sheet as a Document

lessons.title: Reading a Real Indian Angel Term Sheet, Clause by Clause

children.text: So far Rohan has only seen fragments of ChaiCart's term sheet: the binding-effect clause and the exclusivity clause in Lesson 1.1. Now he has the full document in front of him, six pages, numbered clauses, a schedule attached. It looks intimidating until you realise it is really just four or five familiar ideas, repeated in slightly different words every time.

body.text: Every term sheet's clauses sort into a handful of buckets: who is involved and how much money moves, the economics of the deal, who controls what afterward, terms that attach personally to founders, and the legal process terms that make the document work. Learn the buckets once, and no term sheet looks unfamiliar again.

children.text: The Buckets of Any Term Sheet
Before reading ChaiCart's term sheet line by line, it helps to know where each clause is headed, and where in this course you will find the detail behind it.

body.caption: The five buckets, and where this course covers each one

cells: Parties, investment amount, instrument, valuation, cap table representation, use of proceeds
Liquidation preference, redemption, conversion, anti-dilution, pro-rata rights
Board seats, observer rights, protective provisions, information rights
Founder vesting, non-compete, right of first refusal, co-sale, drag-along
A later chapter of this course
Binding effect, confidentiality, exclusivity, conditions precedent, governing law

body.label: How long is a typical Indian angel term sheet
body.context: Longer than a US seed-stage SAFE (1 to 2 pages), because it fixes a valuation and negotiates real terms, but shorter than an institutional Series A term sheet from a VC fund, which can run past 10 pages once side letters are attached.

children.text: Bucket 1: Deal Mechanics, Clause by Clause

This bucket sets up the deal before anyone argues about economics or control. It usually appears first in the document, and it is the one bucket this course has not yet walked through clause by clause.
Parties
"This Term Sheet is entered into between ChaiCart Technologies Private Limited (the \"Company\"), its Promoters, Ananya Rao and Vikram Shah, and Rohan Mehta (the \"Investor\")."

Notice that Ananya and Vikram are named personally, not just "the Company." Some obligations later in the document, founder vesting and non-compete among them, attach to individuals, not to ChaiCart. If a founder is not named as a party here, those personal obligations may not bind them at all.
Investment Amount and Instrument
"The Investor shall subscribe to 625 Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares (\"CCPS\") of face value ₹10 each, for an aggregate consideration of ₹20,00,000 (Rupees Twenty Lakh only)."

This is the clause that fixes the instrument, covered in the previous lesson, and the exact numbers behind it. Only ₹10 of face value per share, ₹6,250 in total, gets recorded as share capital. The rest is securities premium.

stats.label: Securities premium
stats.context: The bulk of what Rohan actually pays

children.text: Pre-Money and Post-Money Valuation

"The pre-money valuation of the Company is agreed at ₹4,00,00,000 (Rupees Four Crore) on a fully diluted basis, and the post-money valuation, after giving effect to this round, shall be ₹5,00,00,000 (Rupees Five Crore)."
The phrase "on a fully diluted basis" is worth pausing on. It means the
₹4 crore already accounts for every outstanding option and convertible instrument, not just the shares currently on the register

. Founders sometimes ask to expand the ESOP pool right before a round closes. If that expansion happens pre-money, the extra dilution falls on the founders, not on Rohan. If it happens post-money instead, Rohan absorbs a share of it too.

body.text: As the investor, this is one of the few deal-mechanics points actually worth negotiating: ask, in writing, whether any promised ESOP top-up is being carved out of the pre-money valuation or the post-money valuation. It is a single sentence in the term sheet that decides who pays for it.

body.title: Recomputing Post-Money
body.prompt: Suppose ChaiCart's round size had been ₹1.2 crore instead of ₹1 crore, at the same ₹4 crore pre-money valuation. What would the post-money valuation be, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Post-money valuation is always pre-money plus the new money raised: ₹4 crore + ₹1.2 crore = ₹5.2 crore. The round size is the only thing that changed here, so it flows straight through to the post-money figure.

children.text: Capitalisation Representation

"The Company represents that its capitalisation table, as set out in Schedule A, is true, complete and accurate as of the date of this Term Sheet, and that the fully diluted share capital, including all outstanding CCDs, options and convertible instruments, is accurately reflected therein."

This clause exists so that Rohan cannot be blindsided by dilution he did not know about. If ChaiCart had raised an undisclosed CCD bridge round before this Series A, the way Verve Fitness did in the previous lesson, this is the clause that would obligate ChaiCart to disclose it upfront, as Schedule A, rather than let Rohan discover it after his money is already in.
Use of Proceeds

"The proceeds of this investment shall be utilised primarily for store expansion, working capital and technology development, and shall not be used for repayment of promoter loans or personal expenses of the Promoters, except as expressly agreed in writing."

This is a commitment about how the money gets spent, and it becomes genuinely enforceable once the information rights covered in Chapter 3 give Rohan visibility into ChaiCart's actual spending through quarterly financials and budgets.
Validity Period
"This Term Sheet shall remain open for acceptance until 5:00 PM IST on the date falling seven days from the date hereof, after which it shall automatically lapse if not executed by all parties."

Do not confuse this with the long-stop date from Lesson 1.1. The validity period is the clock on the unsigned offer itself, before anyone has signed. The long-stop date is a separate clock that starts only after signing, governing how long the parties have to actually close the deal.

body.text: Buckets 2 to 5, economics, control and governance, founder and exit terms, and process and legal, are exactly what the map at the top of this lesson pointed you to. The rest of this course walks through each of them in the same clause-by-clause style used here.

children.text: The Pre-Signing Checklist

body.title: Before You Sign Any Term Sheet
steps: Confirm the exact instrument, CCPS, CCD or SAFE/iSAFE, and check it against the cap table it implies.
Confirm the pre-money valuation and whether it is stated on a fully diluted basis, including any promised ESOP top-up.
Check whether any ESOP pool expansion happens pre-money (diluting founders) or post-money (diluting everyone, including you).
Read the binding-effect clause and note exactly which clauses are carved out as binding.
Find the exclusivity/no-shop period and its exact start and end dates.
Find the confidentiality clause and check how long it survives after signing.
Confirm the capitalisation representation and ask for the actual cap table as a schedule, not just a promise that one exists.
Check the use-of-proceeds clause against what you were told verbally about how the money will be spent.
Note the term sheet's own validity period, separate from the deal's long-stop date.
Confirm the governing law and dispute resolution forum.

children.text: Try It: Which Bucket Does This Clause Belong To

body.title: Classify This Clause
body.question: "For 12 months following Closing, no Promoter shall, directly or indirectly, engage in or provide services to any business competing with the Company's business in India." Which bucket does this clause belong to?
body.explanation: A non-compete binds a founder personally, not the company or its economics, so it sits in the Founder & Exit Terms bucket, covered in a later chapter of this course.

body.title: Classify This Clause
body.question: "The Company shall provide the Investor with unaudited quarterly financial statements and an annual budget within 30 days of each quarter end." Which bucket does this clause belong to?
body.explanation: This is an information right, which governs what an investor gets to see after investing. It belongs to the Control & Governance bucket, covered in Chapter 3 of this course.

cards.definition: The clause naming who is bound by the term sheet. Founders are often named personally, not just the company, because some obligations attach to individuals.
A valuation or ownership figure calculated as if every outstanding option and convertible instrument had already converted into shares.
Whether a promised ESOP pool expansion is added pre-money (founders bear the dilution) or post-money (all shareholders, including new investors, share it).
A clause where the company confirms its cap table, including all convertible instruments, is accurate and complete as disclosed.
A clause restricting how the invested money can be spent, often excluding repayment of promoter loans or personal expenses.
The deadline for the unsigned term sheet itself to be accepted, distinct from the long-stop date that governs closing after signing.

points: A term sheet's clauses sort into five buckets: deal mechanics, economics, control and governance, founder and exit terms, and process and legal terms.
Deal mechanics clauses, parties, investment amount, instrument, valuation and cap table representation, set up the deal before anyone negotiates economics or control.
Always check whether a stated valuation is on a fully diluted basis, and whether any promised ESOP top-up is added pre-money or post-money, since that detail decides who bears the dilution.
A capitalisation representation obligates the company to disclose any prior convertible instruments, such as an earlier CCD bridge round, rather than let you discover them after investing.
A term sheet's own validity period, when the unsigned offer lapses, is a different clock from the long-stop date, when the signed deal lapses if it does not close in time.
Reading a real term sheet is pattern recognition: once you know which bucket a clause belongs to, you know how negotiable it is and where to look for the detail.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal or investment advice. ChaiCart, its founders and Rohan are fictional, and the clause language shown is illustrative rather than a template for a real transaction. Term sheet drafting varies by deal and should always be reviewed by a qualified lawyer before signing. Startup investments are high risk, illiquid, and can result in the loss of your entire capital.
